To assess whether this increased reliance on mental models reflected increasingly accurate knowledge of the task structure, we measured explicit knowledge of the task structure through posttask questions targeting the relationships between gnomes and forests. Initial task knowledge was similiar between conditions (language: M = 0.06; observation: M = 0.02; t(196.08) = 1.79, p = 0.08, 95% CI = [-0.00, 0.08]), but increased across generations only in the language condition (𝛽𝛽 = 0.05, SE = 0.00, t(1996) = 20.06, p < 0.001, 95% CI = [0.05, 0.06]), remaining near floor levels in the observation condition (𝛽𝛽 = 0.00, SE = 0.00, t(1996) = 1.2, p = 0.27, 95% CI = [-0.00, 0.01]; Generation × Condition: β = 0.05, SE = 0.00, t(1996) = 13.41, p < 0.001, 95% CI = [0.04, 0.06];

Fig. 2C and Supplementary Table 8). Critically, in the language condition, demonstrators' task knowledge predicted learners' subsequent knowledge (β = 0.51, SE = 0.02, t(584.00) = 24.71, p < 0.001, 95% CI = [0.47, 0.55]), performance (β = 0.73, SE = 0.06, t(543.80) = 11.73, p < 0.001, 95% CI = [0.61, 0.85]) and model reliance (β = 0.15, SE = 0.01, t(516.90) = 11.91, p < 0.001, 95% CI = [0.13, 0.18]). We detected no comparable transmission effects in the observation condition (see Supplementary Information section 1.6), indicating that language, but not observation, reliably transmitted knowledge of the environment's underlying structure.

We next asked whether the absence of cumulative improvement in the observation condition could simply reflect insufficient information in the demonstrations. To address this, we constructed a Bayesian ideal observer (see Supplementary Information section 2.4). The ideal observer was exposed to the same human-generated transitions that participants observed and had access to the correct representational space, tracking gnome color rather than task-irrelevant features. Across a range of prior assumptions, it readily acquired high task knowledge, demonstrating that the observed behavior contained sufficient information, in principle, to recover the hidden structure (see Supplementary Information Section 2.4). Human observers nevertheless failed to do so reliably, suggesting that their difficulty reflected how this information was inferred or represented rather than its availability.

Cumulative improvement requires sufficiently faithful transmission of structural knowledge

What level of transmission fidelity is required for increasingly accurate mental models to accumulate across generations? To address this, we implemented a simplified agent-based model (see Methods). Across ten generations, agents inherited two attributes from a single demonstrator selected via the same procedure used for participants: task knowledge and model reliance, initialized from the corresponding empirical distributions (see Methods). Two processes governed how attributes changed between generations. First, transmission was imperfect: inherited attributes were degraded by noise proportional to a transmission fidelity parameter, capturing information lost or distorted in passing from demonstrator to learner. Second, agents could revise their inherited attributes through individual learning, modeled as stochastic perturbation (see Methods). The simulations reproduced the qualitative empirical pattern and revealed a strong dependence on transmission fidelity: task knowledge and model reliance accumulated across generations only when fidelity was sufficiently high; at lower levels, both remained essentially flat (Fig. 2D). This extends existing accounts of transmission fidelity in cumulative culture 19, 27, 42 by specifying what must be preserved: when behavior does not readily reveal the underlying structure, information supporting an accurate mental model must be transmitted with sufficient fidelity. To characterize how mental models were expressed and progressively refined across generations, we analyzed the content of written advice in the language condition (Fig. 3). First, we computed semantic similarity scores between all pairs of advice texts using a pre-trained language model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence transformer 43 ), yielding scores from -1 (opposite) to 1 (nearly identical content). Messages became increasingly similar across generations (β = 0.02https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?e7b1YZ t( 7 To identify what messages were converging on, we used BERTopic 44 , a data-driven modeling technique using pre-trained transformer embeddings to capture semantic relationships without incorporating task information. This method identified six larger thematic clusters (Fig. 3B-C, Supplementary Information section 4.2). Two clusters (Topics 2 and 4) were characterized by structurally informative content, including references to the second stage of the task (e.g., the different forests and their associated basket colors) and strategies for switching between forests as their relative value changed (Fig. 3K shows an example message classified as Topic 2). Although lexically distinct, these two topics were highly similar semantically, suggesting that they captured related representations of the same underlying structure (Fig. 3C).

Transmitted mental models become more accurate across generations

Receiving advice from these topics predicted better performance (Topic 2: β = 0.20, SE = 0.03, t(860.8) = 5.73, p < 0.001, 95% CI = [0.13, 0.27]; Topic 4: β = 0.18, SE = 0.03, t(892.7) = 5.50, p < 0.001, 95% CI = [0.12, 0.25]; Fig. 3G and Supplementary Table 18), higher task knowledge (Topic 2: β = 0.43, SE = 0.03, t(884.0) = 14.39, p < 0.001, 95% CI = [0.37, 0.49]; Topic 4: β = 0.37, SE = 0.03, t(897.9) = 12.72, p < 0.001, 95% CI = [0.32, 0.43]; Fig. 3H and Supplementary Table 19), and greater model-reliance (Topic 2: β = 0.20, SE = 0.03, t(870.99) = 5.84, p < 0.001, 95% CI = [0.13, 0.27]; Topic 4: β = 0.19, SE = 0.03, t(894.8) = 5.67, p < 0.001, 95% CI = [0.12, 0.25]; Fig. 3I and Supplementary Table 20), see Supplementary Information Section 1.8 for additional results.

The prevalence of these topics increased systematically across generations (Topic 2: OR = 1.44, FDR-adjusted p < 0.001, 95% CI [1.34, 1.58]; Topic 4: OR = 1.17, FDR-adjusted p < 0.001, 95% CI [1.08, 1.28]; Fig. 3D-F and Supplementary Table 32). Conversely, receiving advice from Topics 0, 1, 3, and 5 predicted lower knowledge of the underlying task structure, and Topics 0 and 1 also predicted lower task performance (see Supplementary Information section 1.8). The prevalence of these topics declined across generations (see Fig. 3D-F; Supplementary Information section 4.3 and Supplementary Table 32). Consistent with payoff-sensitive selection favoring lineages carrying structurally informative content, lineages whose messages fell within Topics 2 and 4 expanded disproportionately (Fig. 3J). Next, we took a complementary, top-down approach, using a large language model (LLM) classifier to rate each written message along multiple criteria (Fig 4A). The key goal was to quantify how accurately advice reflected the underlying task structure (Fig. 4). LLM ratings strongly agreed with independent human ratings on the same criteria (ICCs = 0.60-0.89, all p < .001; see

Supplementary Information Section 5.1 & 5.2 for additional information).

This analysis revealed a dual process of refinement: accurate content accumulated while incorrect and irrelevant content was filtered out across generations. Advice increasingly referenced the relationships determining which gnomes (first state) led to which forests (second state, 'state transitions', β = 0.12, SE = 0.01, t(998) = 16.87, p < 0.001, 95% CI = [0.11, 0.14]; see Supplementary Table 42) and the drifting reward structure (β = 0.08, SE = 0.01, t(998) = 9.22, p < 0.001, 95% CI = [0.06, 0.10]; see Supplementary Table 42), and receiving such advice messages predicted both higher performance and greater knowledge of the task structure (Fig. 4C-D, see Supplementary Information section 1.9). Conversely, incorrect content -typically false mappings between specific figure colors and rewards -and task-irrelevant content declined across generations (see Supplementary Information Section 5.3 & 5.4). Receiving advice with more such content predicted reduced performance, lower task knowledge, and less model reliance, indicating that the transmission process actively filtered content that impeded improvement (Fig 4C-D, see Supplementary Information Section 1.9). One alternative explanation is that cumulative improvement arose through selection among advice topics: more informative topics may simply have become more common across generations, without the content of those topics improving. To distinguish this from genuine refinement, we examined how advice messages evolved within Topics 2 and 4. Within both clusters, references to the transition structure and reward variability increased across generations, while incorrect and irrelevant content declined (see Supplementary Information section 5.4, Supplementary Fig. 20).

Thus, cumulative improvement reflected not only selection among message variants, but also progressive refinement of their content 27, 42.

Discussion

Our results isolate a fundamental challenge for cultural transmission: observing successful behavior does not necessarily reveal the underlying structure that makes it successful. Because the same behavior can be consistent with multiple explanations, learners must infer which features and relationships matter. Our findings show that language can reduce this ambiguity by communicating information about that structure, allowing increasingly accurate mental models to accumulate across generations and supporting cumulative gains in performance.

Prior work has shown that cumulative improvement can occur even without causal understanding when behavior transparently reveals what is worth copying 4, 8, 45, 46 . Our task removed this scaffolding: Similar actions and outcomes could arise from different underlying representations of the underlying task structure 47, 48 . Although observed actions contained sufficient information for an ideal Bayesian observer to learn the task structure, human learners did not reliably infer or transmit that structure across generations. This points to a problem distinct from information sufficiency. Observation can provide evidence compatible with multiple mental models without specifying which features and relationships should be treated as meaningful 14, 49 . This problem is closely related to function and structure learning, in which learners must infer the latent relationships generating observed input-output pairs from among multiple plausible alternatives 50, 51 . Language can reduce this inferential problem by explicitly identifying the dimensions that matter (here, gnome color), constraining the space of models learners must consider.

Messages were not simply copied but progressively transformed. Across generations, content reflecting the task's underlying relationships became more prevalent, whereas incorrect and task-irrelevant content declined. This change reflected both selection among transmitted advice variants and refinement within them: structurally informative message types became more common, while the content of those same message types also became increasingly accurate. Moreover, receiving structurally informative messages predicted greater explicit knowledge, better performance, and increased reliance on model-based strategies, linking the content of cultural transmission to the decision processes that supported successful behavior.

Cumulative improvement therefore depended on preserving enough structural information for subsequent learners to construct and refine accurate mental models. The agent-based model formalized this requirement: cumulative improvement emerged only when task-relevant information was transmitted with sufficient fidelity to support continued refinement across generations. Below this threshold, neither task knowledge nor model reliance accumulated. Existing accounts treat transmission fidelity as a prerequisite for cumulative culture without always specifying what must be preserved 52 . Our results suggest that when successful behavior does not readily reveal the underlying structure, transmission must preserve enough information about that structure for accurate mental models to be reconstructed and improved. Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, our task was designed so that the underlying structure was compact, stable, and readily expressible in language. Whether the same advantage holds in more complex and naturalistic tasks, where relevant relationships may be noisier, higher-dimensional, or less readily verbalized, remains an open question. Transmission of knowledge of hidden relationships in those contexts may require other forms of symbolic representation, such as maps or diagrams. Second, performance-based selection was imposed by the experimental design rather than arising endogenously. Unlike standard transmission chains in which each participant simply becomes a model for the next 53https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?DchyNY 54 , our design allows higher-performing individuals to contribute disproportionately to subsequent generations. This captures a selective consequence that can arise through several cultural-evolutionary processes-including differential survival or reproduction, vertical transmission when more successful individuals leave more biological or cultural descendants, and payoff-biased demonstrator choice-while ensuring that the strength of selection was identical across the language and observation conditions. At the same time, the design does not capture additional dynamics that may arise when learners themselves choose among multiple potential models https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?DkKe92 . Third, our analyses do not specify how learners reconstruct and extend mental models from the advice they receive. In the agent-based model, this process was deliberately abstracted as stochastic variation in task knowledge and model reliance rather than modelled as a cognitive mechanism. Future work should examine how linguistic input is transformed into new or revised internal representations. Models of insight 55 https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?SPaMMD hypothesis generation, or program induction 56, 57 may provide useful starting points for formalizing this process. Finally, mental models were inferred, rather than directly measured (e.g., with brain imaging 58, 59 ), through converging behavioral, computational, and linguistic measures, and our agent-based model intentionally reduced this richer description to simplified attributes capturing task knowledge and model reliance. Future work could test whether similar cumulative refinement occurs with richer, less easily verbalized knowledge and under more naturalistic forms of social selection and interaction.

In summary, our results suggest that when observing successful behavior does not reveal which features and relationships make it work, language can enable increasingly accurate mental models to accumulate across generations 19, [60] [61] [62] . This problem is likely to arise in many domains of human expertise, where successful performance depends on relationships that are not directly visible in expert behavior-from navigation and engineering to medicine. By making such hidden structure communicable, language may allow culture to accumulate not only successful behaviors, but the knowledge that makes them work. This capacity may be one reason human cumulative culture reaches forms of complexity rarely seen in other species [63] [64] [65] . completed trials (of 256). Following the task, participants answered questionnaires designed to assess their knowledge of the task's hidden structure.

Decision-making task

Participants completed a computerized modified two-step sequential decision task 32https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?6YHFFj 33 , framed as a "mushroom picking" game. Each participant performed 256 trials, with an optional break of up to 5 minutes every 64 trials.

On each trial, participants were presented with a pair of "gnome" figures in a village scene. Across the experiment, there were eight unique gnomes arranged into four fixed pairs. Gnomes differed along two dimensions: size (tall or small) and color (brown, purple, pink, green, red, yellow, blue, or orange). Pairs of gnomes remained constant throughout the task, but their on-screen position (left or right) was randomized on each trial. Pair composition and presentation order were randomized independently for each participant in the first generation. From the second generation onward, participants inherited the pair composition of their direct demonstrator.

Participants had 1,500ms to select one gnome by pressing the "S" key (left) or the "K" key (right).

Following the selection, the participant was taken to one of two forest scenes (dark or bright), each containing a colored basket (red or yellow). As with gnome pairs, the forest-basket combination was fixed for the duration of the task and inherited from the participant's demonstrator starting in the second generation. On this screen, participants had 1,500ms to press the spacebar to collect rewards, represented as mushrooms.

In both stages, visual feedback was provided in the form of a white rectangle highlighting the chosen stimulus for the remainder of the response window. The participant's objective was to collect as many mushrooms as possible.

Following 33 https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?HgqVbo each trial included a stakes manipulation: in 50% of trials, rewards were multiplied by 5 ("high-stakes" condition), and in the remaining trials, rewards were multiplied by 1 ("low-stakes" condition). Reward followed a Gaussian random walk (σ = 2 points) bounded between 0 and 9, and was then multiplied by the stake. The number of mushrooms obtained was displayed for 2 s after each successful trial, and the participant's cumulative score was continuously visible in the top-right corner of the screen.

Crucially, the task was governed by a hidden relational structure that was never disclosed to participants. The transition from a gnome to a forest was deterministic and determined solely by the gnome's color: of the eights gnomes, four lead to one forest and four to the other. Each pair consisted of one gnome leading to each forest, so that on every trial the choice between the two gnomes was effectively a choice between the two forests. A gnome's size and on-screen position were irrelevant to the transition. Because mushrooms were obtained at the forests and their yield drifted over time (see above), the more rewarding forest changed across the task. Therefore, good task performance required learning the latent color-to-forest mapping and continuously tracking which forest currently yielded more mushrooms.

Experimental conditions

Starting the second generation, participants were assigned to either the Language or the Observation condition. The first generation was identical for both conditions.

In the Language condition, participants read a written piece of advice provided by a unique demonstrator before the main task. To ensure that they carefully read the advice, participants were asked to write a short summary of it in their own words immediately after reading (average embedding similarity between the received advice and the written summary was 0.67, indicating strong alignment; see Supplementary Information section 4.1 for the similarity method). Reading time was not restricted. After completing the main task, participants were then asked to provide advice themselves. They were incentivized to produce informative advice through a monetary bonus based on the performance of the subsequent participant who received their advice. Writing time was unlimited, and advice was constrained to a maximum of 2,000 characters.

In the Observation condition, participants watched the task replay of the last 80 completed trials (i.e., trials that gave a reward) of their demonstrator before the main task. The replay included the entire choice and reward sequence for each trial, and used the real response times of the demonstrator. This observation phase lasted approximately 18 minutes. To ensure that participants attended these trials, we implemented attention checks. In random trials, participants had to either reproduce the choice made by their demonstrator or indicate the number of rewards they obtained (i.e., either > 5 or ≤ 5). Participants who failed more than five attention checks were removed from the experiment. After the observation phase and before the main task, participants were informed that they would also be recorded. Consistent with the Language condition, participants were incentivized to produce informative demonstration trials through a monetary bonus based on the performance of the subsequent participants who would watch their trials. On the last break screen during the main task, participants were reminded that the recording would start immediately afterwards.

Procedure

Participants first viewed a sequence of screens presenting the task instructions, timing, estimated time, and financial compensation through text and illustrative figures. The instructions were designed to provide the information necessary to perform the task correctly while minimizing information about the underlying task structure. All instruction texts and figures are available in the online data repository (https://osf.io/e92q4/overview?view_only=9edea7d5b894444bb9c305dd19f53c40).

Following the instruction phase, participants completed a practice session to familiarize themselves with the task. This session consisted of 20 trials. Except for the village background in the first stage, all stimuli used in the practice trials differed from those in the main task to avoid inducing any bias toward specific stimuli. In these trials, second-stage outcomes had fixed values: one forest consistently offered a high number of mushrooms (between 5 and 9), while the other offered a low number (between 0 and 4). Participants received feedback whenever they failed to respond within the allotted time, consisting of a message indicating that their response was too slow and a reminder of the correct response key for that screen. Participants were not excluded based on their performance in the practice trials.

After the practice session, participants in generations 2-10 completed a social learning phase. During this phase, they received information from one of their direct demonstrators.

Participants in generation 1 did not complete this phase and proceeded directly to the main task. In the Language condition, the transmitted information consisted of written advice provided by the demonstrator. In the Observation condition, participants watched the last 80 successful trials of their demonstrator's task performance.

Following the social learning phase, participants completed the main task, consisting of 256 trials of a two-step sequential decision task adapted from 32 . Performance on these trials determined participants' total score and performance-based bonus compensation. After completing the main task, participants in the Language condition were asked to provide written advice for the next participant.

Finally, participants completed a set of post-task questionnaires. Before beginning, they were instructed on how to provide their responses. The first questionnaire assessed participants' knowledge of each pair of gnomes encountered in the main task. The second assessed their knowledge of the transition between gnomes and forests. For both questionnaires, responses were collected on rating scales. Upon completing the final questionnaire, participants were shown a debriefing screen thanking them for their participation and providing the completion code required to validate their participation on Prolific.

Questionnaires

Participants completed two questionnaires regarding their knowledge of the underlying task structure. For both questionnaires, the participants had to answer on a scale from 0 to 100, along with a confidence rating of their answer on a scale from 0 (not confident at all) to 100 (very confident). Response time was not limited for the questionnaires. Stimuli position and order were randomized.

We assessed how well participants knew that gnomes were shown in fixed pairs, referred to as Pair Knowledge. Participants saw two gnomes on the screen and were asked the question: "How often did these gnomes appear together?". Responses were provided on a scale from 0 (never together) to 100 (always together). This question was asked for all possible combinations of the eight gnome stimuli, resulting in 28 items. Results for Pair Knowledge are reported in the Supplementary Information section 1.

We assessed how well participants knew that the gnome-to-forest transitions were fixed (i.e., each gnome always led to the same forest), referred to as Transition Knowledge (the task knowledge measure used in the main text and following analyses). Participants saw a gnome and a forest on the screen and were asked the question: "How often did selecting this particular gnome lead you to this pictured forest?" Responses were provided on a scale from 0 (never led to) to 100 (always led). This question was asked for all possible combinations of the eight gnome stimuli and two forest stimuli, resulting in 16 items.

For all items, we inverted the scale so that 100 always corresponded to the correct answer.

All responses were then normalized on a scale from -1 (incorrect) to 1 (correct), with 0 representing uncertainty. Finally, we averaged responses across all items for both questionnaires, resulting in two scores.

Selection algorithm

From the second generation, participants were automatically assigned a demonstrator from the preceding generation. This demonstrator was selected by deterministic tournament selection, a fitness-based selection algorithm used in genetic algorithms 39 with k = 4. To compute fitness, we first applied z-score standardization to the task performance score and then rescaled these scores to a [0, 1] range using min-max normalization.

Exclusion criteria

Participants who completed fewer than 80% of trials (i.e., 51 failed trials) were excluded from the experiment. A trial was considered failed if the participant provided no response or if the response time was shorter than 200ms. Similarly, participants who answered fewer than 80% of the questionnaire items were excluded. Participants who did not provide advice or whose advice was judged inappropriate (containing profanity or sexism) in manual prescreening were also removed from the experiment.

We overrecruited participants by 30% to account for possible exclusions. This occasionally resulted in generations where more than 100 participants passed the exclusion criteria. In such cases, a random subset was removed to maintain exactly 100 participants per generation.

Statistical analysis

All analyses were conducted using the software R v.4.5.2. When analyzing differences between experimental conditions in the first and last generation, we used the Welch two-sample t-test. To analyze the evolution of behavioral variables (task performance, task knowledge, pair knowledge and model reliance) as well as the linguistic variables (BERTopic thematic clusters and message features from the language analysis), we used linear regression models. When comparing the impact of condition on the growth of the behavioral variables, we fitted linear regression models with the variable of interest as a dependent variable, condition as a fixed effect, and generation as a continuous variable. For all linear models, we report 95% confidence intervals. To compute the impact of the linguistic variables on the behavioral variables, we used linear mixed models implemented with the lmer package 66 . It included the linguistic variables as a fixed effect, with a random intercept by generation, and used a Gaussian error distribution. Except for generation, all variables were z-scored for this analysis. To analyze how the prevalence of each topic changed across generations, we used one-vs-rest logistic regression: for each topic, we fitted a standard logistic regression model predicting the binary outcome of whether a given response was assigned to that topic, with generation as the fixed effect. We report unstandardized estimates as effect sizes, together with the corresponding odds ratio. P-values were corrected for multiple comparisons across topics using the FDR method.

Reinforcement learning model

We modeled first-stage choices (selecting a gnome) using a performance-based arbitration model in which model-based (MB) and model-free (MF) controllers jointly determine choice, with their relative influence varying according to their recent performance 41, 67, 68 . The MF controller learns cached action values from experienced rewards, whereas the MB controller evaluates actions prospectively using the participant's inferred model of the task's transition structure. As a result, greater reliance on MB control is expected when that internal model provides more accurate predictions than the MF strategy.

On trial t in the first-stage states, each controller's action values were transformed into a softmax choice policy, and the two policies are mixed by a state-specific arbitration weight wt(s): where X ∈ {MB, MF}.

The arbitration weight was determined by the difference of the two controllers' running estimates of the performance, where η1 sets the sensitivity to the performance difference, and η0 sets a baseline bias towards either 1 controller (η0 > 0 favors MF control).

After each outcome, the performance estimate of each controller for the visited state was updated 3 toward the obtained reward rt, weighted by that controller's responsibility for the chosen action:

Thus, control shifted dynamically toward the controller whose choices had more recently been 5 associated with reward in that state.

6

The MF controller learns cached values by temporal-difference learning. The value of the chosen 7 first-stage action was updated toward the value of the second-stage state reached, s2, and that value 8 is updated toward the reward. The second-stage reward prediction error was additionally propagated 9 back to the first-stage action through an eligibility trace λ:

The MB controller instead computed values prospectively from the transition model and the current 11 values of the second-stage states: 12

The accuracy of the participant's transition model was governed by a task-knowledge parameter u, 13 shared across first-stage states. A value of u = 1 corresponds to a correct transition structure, u = 0.5 14 to no systematic structural knowledge, and u < 0.5 to an inverted transition model. Because u was inferred from participants' choices, it is distinct from the explicit task-knowledge measure obtained from the post-task questionnaire; their correspondence is shown in Supplementary Fig. 9.

The model had eight free parameters: inverse temperature β, reward learning rate α, performance learning rates αMB and αMF, eligibility trace λ, arbitration bias η0, arbitration sensitivity η1, and task knowledge u. Parameters were estimated separately for each participant by maximum likelihood.

To reduce the risk of local optima, optimization was repeated from 100 starting points sampled uniformly within the parameter bounds, and the solution with the highest log-likelihood was retained.

The model-reliance measure w reported in the Results was derived from the fitted model rather than estimated as a free parameter. For each participant, we simulated the model with their best-fitting parameters on their own trial sequence, recorded the trial-wise arbitration weight wt, and averaged it within participants. This measure therefore summarizes the participant's average reliance on MB control implied by the fitted arbitration process over the task they actually experienced.

As a robustness check, we also fit a conventional hybrid reinforcement-learning model in which a single fixed model-based weight w was estimated as a free parameter and used to combine MB and MF values throughout the task 32 . This model produced the same qualitative increase in model reliance across generations; results are reported in Supplementary Fig. 11.

Agent-based model

Agents were organized into 𝐺𝐺 = 10 discrete generations, each consisting of 𝑁𝑁 = 100 agents. As in the behavioral experiment, agents in generation 𝑔𝑔 > 1 inherited their attributes from a single demonstrator in the previous generation 𝑔𝑔 -1 and subsequently performed the task.

Each agent was characterized by two attributes: 𝑚𝑚, representing task knowledge (analogous to participant task knowledge), and 𝑤𝑤, representing the degree of model-reliance (analogous to the variable 𝑤𝑤 estimated for participants; see Reinforcement Learning model). The first generation was initialized from participants' behavioural data. Selection for transmission followed the same tournament selection algorithm used in the experiment. To model differences in transmission fidelity across experimental conditions, stochastic noise was introduced during the inheritance of 𝑚𝑚 which ranges from 0 (maximum noise) to 1 (perfect transmission). For all visualizations, we selected five transmission quality levels (0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00) by identifying parameter combinations (𝛼𝛼 𝑇𝑇 , 𝛽𝛽 𝑇𝑇 ) that produced these expected values.

Each agent could modify its inherited attributes, analogous to individual learning in the behavioral experiment. Agents updated their attributes with probability 𝑒𝑒. Learning was implemented as additive Gaussian noise: where

To assess how transmission fidelity and learning influenced cultural evolution, we ran the agentbased simulation for a grid of 4 parameters: 𝛼𝛼 𝑇𝑇 , 𝛽𝛽 𝑇𝑇 , 𝑒𝑒 and 𝜎𝜎. Specifically, we used 6 linearly spaced values for 𝛼𝛼 𝑇𝑇 and 𝛽𝛽 𝑇𝑇 from 0.00001 to 5, and 6 linearly spaced values for 𝑒𝑒 and 𝜎𝜎 from 0 to 1. The model was run for 50 simulations for each parameter combination. The results of these sensitivity analyses are shown in Supplementary Figs. 15 16 17.

Topic modeling

To identify common topics and trends in the written messages of participants, we used BERTopic 44 on the raw written messages. Each message was treated as a single document and was embedded with the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence transformer. Embeddings were reduced with UMAP and clustered with HDBSCAN. The resulting topics were labeled after human inspection using the representative terms extracted using class-based TF-IDF. Hyperparameters were selected via grid search using standard metrics of topic coherence, topic diversity, silhouette score, and intra-topic embedding similarity. The final model was chosen where gains in coherence and diversity plateaued while silhouette score remained acceptable. The full pipeline specification is reported in Table S26 and the tuning procedure in Supplementary Section 3.2.1. We report topics with more than 50 messages in the main text. All analyses were replicated using the full set of topics (Supplementary

Information section 1.8 and Supplementary Information section 4.3).

To ensure that our results are not dependent on the set of messages that were classified, we also replicated all analyses after forcing BERTopic to assign all messages (i.e., outliers) to a cluster (Supplementary Information section 4.4). The code implementation can be found in the online repository (https://github.com/DrBlublu/Transmission-of-model-project).

To examine how topics changed across generations, we conducted logistic regression for each topic using a one-vs-rest approach. For each topic, we coded participants as 1 (assigned to that topic) or 0 (assigned to any other topic), then regressed this binary outcome on generation (coded 1-10). This approach tests whether each topic's absolute prevalence increased or decreased across the transmission chain. P-values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using FDR correction 69.

Content analysis

We used Gemini 2.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?a93pCo 70 to analyze the written messages (N = 1,000) based on five criteria: fixed pairs, state transitions, dynamic rewards, color-reward mapping, and irrelevant features. Each criterion was scored on a 0-2 scale (0 = no mention,1 = vague mention,2 = explicit mention). The LLM was provided with detailed scoring rubrics and examples (see Supplementary Table 39 for a description of the criteria). To ensure stability, each text was independently rated 10 times through separate API calls, and scores were averaged to produce the final LLM ratings. To validate the LLM ratings, we compared them against human ratings from five independent judges on a random sample of the corpus (N = 100). We assessed agreement between LLM and humans using intraclass correlation coefficients (see Supplementary Information section 5 for more details).

Participants

We recruited 2,600 participants via Prolific. Eligibility was restricted to participants residing in the United States or the United Kingdom who reported being native English speakers, had normal color vision, and held a Prolific approval rating of at least 95%. Data were collected over 20 sessions from 15/05/2024 to 26/11/2024, with each session beginning at 6:00 PM (GMT+1) on weekdays.

Recruitment aimed to obtain 100 unique participants per generation across ten generations in each of two experimental conditions (100 × 10 ×2 = 2,000), with approximately 30% additional recruitment to offset potential exclusions (see SM 1.9 Exclusion criteria) and technical issues. Each participant was permitted to participate in only one session. Participants were compensated at a base rate of £9 per hour, with the opportunity to earn up to £2 in performance-based bonuses. On average, participants completed the study in under one hour. All participants provided written informed consent before participation. Under the Swedish Ethical Review Act (SFS 2003:460), this type of anonymous, non-invasive research does not fall within the scope of studies requiring ethical review.

Pre-registration and Open Science

Pre-registrations for the studies are available online at https://aspredicted.org/wf6e99.pdf (Language condition) and https://aspredicted.org/7ch2sv.pdf (Observation condition). The preregistration for the language condition specified an adaptive stopping rule based on performance plateauing across generations. In practice, we adopted a fixed design of 10 generations per condition, consistent with standard practice in the transmission chain literature, rather than applying the originally planned stopping criterion. All experimental data, along with the stimuli used in the experiment, the code to implement the experiment, and the analysis code, are available to download from the OSF repository hosted at: https://osf.io/e92q4/overview?view_only=9edea7d5b894444bb9c305dd19f53c40.

Experimental design

Participants took part in an online, multi-generational transmission chain study using a decisionmaking task. Before starting the task, participants had the opportunity to learn from their demonstrator (i.e., the participant who participated in the study before them) through one of two conditions: receiving their written advice or observing the task replay of the demonstrator's last 80 and 𝑤𝑤. Finally, agents were allowed to update their attributes through individual learning before task performance, thereby modifying their inherited attribute values.

To reduce computational complexity, we pre-computed each agent's expected task performance for all combinations of 𝑚𝑚 and 𝑤𝑤 using the same reinforcement learning model that was fit to participant data (see Supplementary Information section 2.2 and Supplementary Information section 3.1 for more information). The resulting performance values were stored in a lookup matrix (Supplementary Fig. 14). Agent performance in the ABM was computed as where 𝑃𝑃𝑒𝑒𝑟𝑟𝑝𝑝𝑃𝑃𝑟𝑟𝑚𝑚𝑎𝑎𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑒𝑒𝑃𝑃𝑎𝑎𝑃𝑃𝑟𝑟𝑃𝑃𝑒𝑒 denotes the pre-computed RL simulation results shown in Supplementary Fig. 14.

To examine the effect of transmission fidelity, inheritance was probabilistic rather than deterministic. Specifically, offspring parameters were scaled by a multiplicative transmission factor drawn from a Beta distribution: where 𝐸𝐸 ∼ 𝐵𝐵𝑒𝑒𝑃𝑃𝑎𝑎(𝛼𝛼 𝑇𝑇 , 𝛽𝛽 𝑇𝑇 ).

The parameters 𝛼𝛼 𝑇𝑇 and 𝛽𝛽 𝑇𝑇 controlled transmission fidelity: values concentrated near 1 correspond to high-fidelity transmission, whereas values concentrated near 0 correspond to noisier transmission.
